content:
There's an old saying in photography: the best camera is the one you have with you. Of course, the iPhone is the camera most of us carry around most of the time, which is a clear advantage for shooting scenes like kids and social events. However, a recent video project helped me notice another benefit of it.

I really enjoy taking an evening stroll through London, often snapping photos and shooting short videos with my iPhone. It started purely as a way to amuse myself, but later I realised these clips could actually serve as B-roll for a video project…

My current project is experimental in nature—meant to test the viability of Cinematic Mode—which is why I lamented earlier that the company seems to have stopped work on it. I'll share the results with you next week.

I plan to use a very specific format that calls for cutting very short scenic B-roll shots into an interview segment. In principle, these shots could be filmed anywhere in London, but since the main scene takes place by the river, I really want all the B-roll to be of the Thames. I needed four such clips, and scrolling through my iPhone footage, I quickly found suitable material.

The clip above also highlights another benefit. If there are passers-by in the frame who might be recognisable, I make a point of approaching them afterwards, showing them the footage, and asking for their consent before using it. (This isn't a legal requirement in the UK, but I consider it basic courtesy.) More often than not, they end up asking me for a copy in return. If they're using an iPhone, AirDrop gets the job done quickly and easily; for Android users, WhatsApp serves as a backup.

The iPhone's image stabilisation is really outstanding—especially given that I wasn't planning to shoot, just out for a walk when I suddenly came across a nice view, so the footage was all handheld. I do try to brace the phone against a wall, railing or lamppost whenever I can, but generally the footage is already very steady as-is, honestly comparable to what you'd get with a tripod. (If I were planning to walk and shoot at the same time, I'd carry a small GorillaPod with me.)

Another big advantage of the iPhone is its grab-and-go nature. If I had to fiddle with exposure, white balance, an ND filter and so on, I'd probably give up shooting altogether—especially when I'm with someone else, the time involved would feel too disruptive. But asking them to wait roughly twenty seconds doesn't really break the rhythm of the walk.

If I want to stop somewhere and shoot for a while, capturing a time-lapse on the iPhone is a breeze. Just hit record, stop whenever I'm ready, and the iPhone handles the rest, outputting a clip of the right length. When I used to live in my old flat, I'd often prop the iPhone by the window at sunset, start a time-lapse, and get on with my own things. Several of those later became very useful B-roll material for the project.

True, if you zoom in pixel by pixel, the limits of the iPhone's small sensor do start to show—especially in low light. But in this day and age when the vast majority of YouTube videos are watched on a phone or laptop, the quality of most of the footage is already more than ample.

Whether Cinematic Mode video reaches the same level is harder to say—you can help me judge that next week. But overall, I'm genuinely amazed at being able to pocket such a powerful camera and have it ready to go anytime, anywhere.
